opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it started with curiosity, but it took me a while to understand what kind of curiosity it was.

When I first got into computer vision, it felt like a puzzle-solving exercise. There was a benchmark, you tried to push the number up, and there was a real sense of satisfaction when something worked. But over time I realized that wasn't what kept me going. What really pulled me in was a more basic question: how does a system come to *see*, to understand the world? Vision is so effortless for us that we take it for granted, yet when you try to build it, you realize how deep the problem is.

Another part of it is that I care about simple ideas. In research I'm drawn to things that are clean, that strip a problem down to what really matters. When you find a design or an insight that's almost embarrassingly simple but works much better than expected, that feeling is addictive. You feel like you've touched something true about the problem rather than just engineering around it.

And I think the motivation has shifted as the field has changed. Now that language models have become so powerful, many people ask whether vision still matters, or whether it's just a plug-in for language. For me that actually sharpened my motivation. I believe intelligence has to be grounded in the physical world, in perception, space, and interaction, and language alone can't fully get you there. So part of what drives me now is a conviction, maybe even a bit of stubbornness, that visual understanding and world modeling are central to the next step, not peripheral.

Finally, there's a very human part. I enjoy working with students and collaborators, watching someone go from confused to suddenly seeing the idea. That shared moment of discovery is a big part of why I'm still doing this. Research can be lonely and full of failure, so the intrinsic motivation has to come from somewhere real. For me it's this mix of curiosity, a taste for simplicity, and a belief that the questions we're working on actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response says it took time to understand what kind of curiosity motivated him, but it does not question whether curiosity was truly his intrinsic motivation or only his explanation of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, the intrinsic motivation really comes down to curiosity about how machines can learn to see and understand the world, and honestly, a lot of it is driven by a sense of dissatisfaction with how things currently work.

I think when I started, computer vision was in this phase where things were changing very fast. ResNet had just come out, and suddenly deep learning could do things we thought were impossible. That moment, where you realize the field is wide open and nobody actually knows the right answer yet, is incredibly attractive. You feel like whatever you do might matter.

But over time, the motivation shifted. It became less about chasing the next benchmark and more about asking: what are the foundational principles? Why does this architecture work and that one doesn't? When I worked on ConvNeXt, for example, the question wasn't really "can we beat transformers." It was "do we actually understand what makes these models good, or are we just following trends?" That kind of question is what keeps me going. I like taking something everyone assumes is settled and poking at it.

And then there's a deeper layer, which is about understanding intelligence itself. Vision is such a fundamental part of how humans and animals learn about the world. A child learns so much before they ever learn language, just by looking and interacting. So I keep coming back to the question of whether we can build systems that learn about the world in that kind of way, through perception, without needing everything to be labeled or described in text. That's a very hard problem, and I don't think we've solved it. In fact, I think a lot of the recent progress in multimodal models has actually papered over how shallow our visual understanding still is.

So if I had to summarize it: the motivation is a mix of curiosity, a bit of stubbornness about not accepting the popular narrative, and a belief that there's something deep about visual intelligence we still don't understand. As long as that gap exists, I'll stay interested.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity as a source of motivation, but does not express uncertainty about whether that was his actual motivation or just his explanation of it.

astra-6.text:
我觉得最核心的还是好奇心，就是你碰到一个问题，会忍不住想：它为什么是这样的？有没有更简单、更本质的解释？这种好奇心会推动你不断往下挖。

比如研究视觉智能，很自然就会产生一个疑问：人看一张图片，好像毫不费力就能理解里面的东西，为什么让机器做到这件事却这么难？你开始尝试一些方法，得到一点结果，但结果往往又带来新的问题。这个过程本身就很吸引我。

而且，研究里让我觉得特别有意思的，常常是预期和结果不一致的时候。一个你觉得应该有效的方法没有用，或者一个很简单的改动反而起了作用，你就会想把它弄明白。对我来说，内在动力大概就是这种想理解问题的冲动：即使暂时没有一个明确的答案，也愿意继续探索。

r001.rationale: The response presents curiosity as its core motivation and describes it confidently. It does not acknowledge uncertainty about whether curiosity was Saining Xie’s actual intrinsic motivation or merely his explanation of it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the motivation comes from curiosity—the feeling that there is something fundamental I don’t understand, and I want to get a little closer to it. In computer vision, that question is very intuitive: we see and understand the world so naturally, but how can a machine learn to do that? Once you start working on it, you realize how much is hidden inside that seemingly simple question.

I also really enjoy the process of turning an intuition into an experiment. You have an idea, you build something, and the result surprises you. Sometimes it works, but often the failure is more interesting because it exposes something wrong with your understanding. That cycle keeps pulling me deeper into research.

So I wouldn’t say intrinsic motivation means always feeling excited. There are long periods of frustration. For me, it means there’s still a question I want to come back to, even when nobody is asking me to work on it.

r001.rationale: The response presents curiosity as his motivation directly and does not express uncertainty about whether that was his actual motivation or just his explanation of it.
